title: Thunderstorms & Lightning
summary: If you can hear thunder, you're close enough to be struck.
quick_actions: Go indoors to a fully enclosed building (not a shed, tent, or covered porch) or a car with a roof.
Stay inside until 30 minutes after the last thunder you hear.
Avoid corded electronics and running water while the storm is overhead.
Lightning can strike over 10 miles from where it's raining - don't wait for rain to take shelter.
more_info: A sturdy building with wiring and plumbing gives the lightning a path to ground other than you. If caught outside with no shelter, avoid open fields, tall isolated objects, and water.

title: Beaufort Wind Scale (Estimating Wind Speed by Eye)
summary: Estimate wind speed just by watching smoke, leaves, trees, and flags - no instruments needed.
quick_actions: Force 0-2 (calm to light breeze, under 7 mph/6 knots): smoke drifts or rises mostly straight up, leaves rustle at most.
Force 4-5 (moderate to fresh breeze, 13-24 mph/11-21 knots): loose paper and dust lift, small trees begin to sway.
Force 7-8 (near gale to gale, 32-46 mph/28-40 knots): whole trees are in motion, walking against the wind takes real effort.
Force 10+ (storm and above, 55+ mph/48+ knots): widespread structural damage becomes likely - this is the range where you should already be sheltering, not still observing.

table.observed_on_land: Smoke drift shows wind direction; vanes still
Wind felt on face; leaves rustle
Leaves and small twigs in constant motion; light flags extend
Dust and loose paper lift; small branches move
Small trees in leaf begin to sway
Large branches move; wind whistles in wires
Whole trees in motion; walking against wind is hard
Twigs break off trees; walking is difficult
Structural damage to roofing/signs becomes possible

more_info: Developed by Francis Beaufort in 1805 and adopted internationally by the World Meteorological Organization - this is a global standard, not a US-specific scale, even though the specific table above is NOAA's own published presentation of it. Useful whenever an anemometer isn't available: matching what you actually see to a Force number gives a genuine, communicable wind-speed estimate.

title: Tornadoes
summary: Get to the lowest, most interior, windowless room you can, right away.
quick_actions: Go to a basement or an interior room/hallway on the lowest floor, away from windows.
Drop, Cover, Hold On: get low, cover your head/neck, hold onto something sturdy.
Put as many walls as possible between yourself and the outside.
In a vehicle: don't try to outrun a tornado - get low, buckle in, cover your head.
more_info: A basement or an ICC-500/FEMA-criteria safe room is best. If no shelter is available, avoid vehicles and mobile homes, which offer little protection.

title: Flooding
summary: Turn Around, Don't Drown - never walk, swim, or drive through flood water.
quick_actions: 6 inches of moving water can knock an adult down; 1 foot can sweep away a car.
Evacuate immediately if told to - never drive around barricades.
If your car is trapped in rising water, get out and get on the roof rather than staying inside.
Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.
more_info: Floodwater can hide washed-out roads, downed lines, and contamination. Most flood deaths are vehicle-related.

title: Earthquakes
summary: Drop, Cover, and Hold On the moment you feel shaking.
quick_actions: Drop onto your hands and knees immediately.
Cover your head and neck with one arm/hand; get under a sturdy table if one is near.
Hold on until the shaking completely stops.
After: expect aftershocks, watch for gas leaks and downed lines, and leave a damaged building carefully.
more_info: Do not run outside during shaking - most injuries happen from falling objects indoors, not building collapse.

title: Wildfire & Smoke
summary: Evacuate immediately if told to; otherwise reduce smoke exposure indoors.
quick_actions: If authorities order evacuation, leave right away - don't wait to see how bad it gets.
Close windows/doors; run a HEPA/MERV-13+ filter if you have one, or seal one room as a clean-air space.
An N95 mask (properly fitted) reduces smoke particle inhalation outdoors.
Monitor local alerts for evacuation routes and shelter locations.
more_info: Wildfire smoke's fine particles are the main health hazard - they irritate eyes/airways and worsen heart/lung conditions. Pregnant people, children, older adults, and anyone with respiratory or heart conditions are at higher risk.

title: Extreme Heat
summary: Recognize heat exhaustion vs. heat stroke - heat stroke is a 911 emergency.
quick_actions: Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, cold/pale/clammy skin, dizziness, nausea - move to cool space, sip water, loosen clothing.
Heat stroke: hot/red/dry skin, confusion, body temp above 103°F - call 911 immediately, cool the person by any means while waiting.
If AC is out, find a library, mall, or official cooling center.
Check on elderly neighbors and anyone without AC - they're at highest risk.
more_info: Heat stroke can be fatal within minutes without cooling and medical care - don't wait to see if symptoms improve.

title: Extreme Cold & Winter Weather
summary: Hypothermia and frostbite both need warmth first - know the signs.
quick_actions: Frostbite: numbness, white/grayish-yellow, firm/waxy skin - rewarm gradually in warm (not hot) water, don't rub.
Hypothermia (temp below 95°F is an emergency): shivering, confusion, slurred speech - warm the chest/neck/head/groin first, keep dry.
Never use a gas stove/oven to heat a room - carbon monoxide risk (see Carbon Monoxide topic).
Limit time outdoors; dress in layers; keep a battery-powered CO detector working.
more_info: Winter storms also raise the risk of car accidents, overexertion heart attacks (e.g. shoveling snow), and CO poisoning from indoor heating workarounds.

title: When the Power Goes Out
summary: Keep freezers/fridges closed and have a plan for medical devices.
quick_actions: Keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed - fridge stays cold ~4 hours, a full freezer ~48 hours.
Turn off/unplug sensitive electronics to avoid surge damage when power returns.
Know how long any powered medical devices/refrigerated medication can go without power.
Use flashlights, not candles, for light (see Alternative Lighting & Fire Safety).
more_info: For anything beyond a few hours, see Food Safety, Generator Safety, and Carbon Monoxide topics before improvising heat, cooling, or refrigeration workarounds.

title: Downed Power Lines
summary: Assume every downed line is live - stay back and call it in.
quick_actions: Stay at least 30-50 feet away from a downed line and anything it's touching (fence, puddle, car, tree).
Never touch a downed line or anything in contact with it, even if it looks dead.
Call 911 or your utility immediately to report it.
If it falls on your car while you're inside, stay inside until utility workers say it's safe - if you must exit, shuffle away with small steps, feet together.
more_info: Electricity from a downed line can energize the ground and nearby puddles, not just the wire itself.

title: Generator Safety
summary: Generators belong outside, far from windows - never in a garage or basement.
quick_actions: Run generators outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows/doors/vents.
Never run a generator in a garage, basement, or carport, even with the door open.
Let the engine cool before refueling - spilled fuel on hot parts can ignite.
Use a battery-powered CO detector indoors whenever a generator is running nearby.
more_info: Look for generators with a built-in CO shutoff feature if buying new.

title: Carbon Monoxide Safety
summary: CO is invisible and odorless - symptoms feel like the flu.
quick_actions: Symptoms: headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, confusion - get to fresh air and call 911 if suspected.
Never run a generator, grill, or camp stove indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.
Never use a gas oven/stovetop to heat a room.
Install and maintain battery-powered CO detectors - people asleep or impaired can die before noticing symptoms.
more_info: Infants, older adults, and people with heart or breathing conditions are at higher risk from lower CO levels.

title: Alternative Lighting & Fire Safety
summary: Use flashlights instead of candles during an outage.
quick_actions: Prefer flashlights, headlamps, or battery/solar lanterns over open flame.
If you must use candles, never leave them unattended and keep them away from anything flammable.
Flameless (battery LED) candles remove the fire risk entirely.
Keep a working smoke detector - fire departments see a real rise in candle fires during outages.
more_info: NFPA data: roughly 20 home candle fires happen every day nationally on average, most started by a candle left too close to something flammable.

title: Water Storage & Boil-Water Advisories
summary: Store 1 gallon per person per day; follow local guidance on advisories.
quick_actions: Store at least 1 gallon per person per day; aim for a 2-week supply (~14 gal/person) if space allows.
Use food-grade containers; tap water generally stores fine without additives if containers are clean.
Boil-water advisory: bring water to a rolling boil for 1 minute (longer at high altitude) before drinking/cooking/brushing teeth.
If flood, chemical, or fuel contamination is suspected, boiling may NOT make water safe - use bottled/approved water instead and follow local health department guidance.
more_info: 1 gallon/person/day is a survival minimum (hydration + basic hygiene), not a comfortable supply - more is better if storage allows.

title: Food Safety During an Outage
summary: When in doubt, throw it out.
quick_actions: A closed fridge keeps food cold ~4 hours; a full freezer ~48 hours (24 hours if half-full).
Discard perishable food held above 40°F for 2+ hours, or anything with an unusual smell, color, or texture.
Keep an appliance thermometer in the fridge/freezer to know the actual temperature if the outage is long.
When power returns, check temperatures before deciding what's safe to keep.
more_info: This applies broadly - meat, dairy, leftovers, and anything perishable. Canned/shelf-stable food is generally unaffected by a power outage itself.

title: Sanitation Without Running Water
summary: Plan for toilets before you need one - poor sanitation spreads disease fast.
quick_actions: A 'twin bucket' system (one for urine, one for solid waste with an absorbent/bag liner) is a common low-tech option.
Urine is generally low-risk and can be diluted and disposed of in soil; solid waste needs to be bagged and handled carefully.
Set up a hand-washing station (water container with a spigot + soap) near the toilet area.
Wash hands after any toilet use and before handling food or water, even more so than normal.
more_info: Loss of running water or sewage service is a common secondary effect of floods, earthquakes, and extended power outages - not just its own separate disaster.

title: Family Emergency Communication Plan
summary: Pick an out-of-town contact - long-distance calls/texts often work when local ones don't.
quick_actions: Choose one out-of-town contact everyone can reach/report in to.
Text, don't talk - texts often get through when voice calls can't (see Communications Outages).
Write down/print emergency contacts and a meeting place - don't rely on a phone that could be dead or lost.
Practice the plan (a test text/call) so everyone knows it actually works before you need it.
more_info: Local phone circuits can jam during a widespread emergency even when the network itself is technically up; a distant contact and text messages route around that more reliably.

title: Evacuation
summary: If told to evacuate, go - don't wait to see how bad it gets.
quick_actions: Follow official evacuation orders promptly; never drive around barricades.
Know at least two routes out of your area in case one is blocked.
Bring your go-bag, medications, and pets (see Pets) - don't plan to come back for them.
Let your out-of-town contact know where you're going if you can.
more_info: Evacuation is warranted for many different hazards - fire, flood, extended power/utility loss, hazardous material releases - not just the 'obvious' ones.

title: Shelter-in-Place vs. Evacuating
summary: Sometimes staying put is safer than trying to leave.
quick_actions: Shelter-in-place when going outside is more dangerous than staying (e.g. airborne contamination, extreme weather already underway).
Evacuate when officials order it, or when a hazard makes staying clearly unsafe (fire approaching, structural damage, rising water).
If unsure and not explicitly ordered either way, use the best information you have - local alerts, what you can see/hear/smell - to judge immediate danger.
Always comply immediately if officials specifically order evacuation or medical treatment.
more_info: Plan for both possibilities in advance - the right call depends on the specific hazard, not a fixed rule.

title: When Phones & Internet Are Down
summary: Text over talk, and know your offline fallback.
quick_actions: Text messages often get through even when voice calls fail - cell networks handle them differently under load.
Keep phones charged and conserve battery (see Battery & Power Conservation) - don't stream or leave apps running.
A local device like this PirateBox works with no internet or cell service at all - it's exactly built for this situation.
Consider a battery/hand-crank NOAA weather radio and, if licensed, amateur radio (see the Radio Reference section) as backups that don't depend on cell towers.
more_info: Cell networks can be overwhelmed (congestion) or physically down (towers without power/backhaul) during a widespread event - both look like "no signal" to you but have different likely durations.

title: Battery & Power Conservation
summary: Assume you won't be able to recharge - make it last.
quick_actions: Lower screen brightness, enable low-power/airplane mode when not actively checking for messages.
Close unused apps and disable background refresh/location services you don't need.
Keep devices out of extreme heat/cold - both reduce battery performance and lifespan.
Prioritize charging communication devices (phone, radio) over convenience devices.
more_info: A phone in airplane mode with Wi-Fi on (to still reach a local network like this PirateBox) uses far less battery than one actively searching for a weak cell signal.

title: Pets in an Emergency
summary: If it's not safe for you to stay, it's not safe for your pet either.
quick_actions: Keep a pet kit: several days of food/water, bowls, leash/carrier, litter/waste bags, and any medications.
Microchip pets and keep ID tags/contact info current in case you're separated.
Identify pet-friendly shelters or a safe location in advance - not every emergency shelter accepts animals.
Never leave pets behind when evacuating - they can end up lost, injured, or worse.
more_info: Keep a current photo of each pet in your kit in case you need to identify or describe them if separated.

title: Ground-to-Air Emergency Signals
summary: Six standardized symbols any search-and-rescue aircrew worldwide is trained to recognize - useful when radio and phones are both out.
quick_actions: Build symbols at least 8 feet (2.4 m) across, in an open area visible from above, using any high-contrast material: rocks, logs, tarps, clothing, or footprints stamped into snow or sand.
V = Require assistance. X = Require MEDICAL assistance (this one takes priority with rescue teams). N = No/Negative. Y = Yes/Affirmative.
F = Require food and water. An arrow shape points rescuers toward the direction you're proceeding.
Straight lines and sharp angles read as deliberate/human-made from the air far better than anything curved or irregular - that contrast against natural terrain is what actually gets noticed.
more_info: This is a real, internationally standardized code (part of the FAA/ICAO search-and-rescue signal set) - not a PirateBox invention, and not the same thing as Morse SOS (see the Radio page), which is an audio/light signal rather than a ground panel. Both are worth knowing since they work in different situations.
source_note: Symbol meanings cross-checked against multiple secondary summaries of the published FAA/ICAO standard rather than the primary AIM/Annex 12 text directly - confidence set to medium on that basis, though the core 6 symbols shown are consistently reported across sources.

title: International Emergency Numbers
summary: 911 is a North American convention, not a global one - know the local number before you need it.
quick_actions: 112 works throughout the European Union (alongside any older national number) and is also recognized in many other countries as a secondary/mobile emergency number.

Most GSM mobile phones will attempt to place a 112 (or sometimes 911) emergency call even when locked or with no SIM card inserted - a useful fallback, but not a guarantee on every device/network/country.
Some countries split services across separate numbers (e.g. Japan: 110 police, 119 fire/ambulance) rather than one combined number - check which service you actually need.

more_info: This is a curated set of major/representative countries, not a complete list - always confirm the actual local number for wherever you are (a hotel, airport, or embassy can usually tell you immediately). The Local Information section of this PirateBox may also have this box's own local emergency numbers configured, if the operator has set that up.

title: Ten Essentials for Outdoor/Field Safety
summary: A standard packing checklist that covers navigation, sun/weather protection, food/water, and emergency shelter for any outdoor trip.
quick_actions: Navigation (map, compass, GPS), sun protection (sunglasses/sunscreen/hat), and extra clothing/layers.
Illumination (flashlight/headlamp), first-aid supplies, and fire-starting (matches/lighter).
A repair kit/tools (knife, duct tape, multi-tool), extra food, and water plus water-treatment supplies.
Emergency shelter (tent, space blanket, tarp, or bivy) - the item most often skipped on a day trip that then runs long.
more_info: None of these require expensive gear - the point is covering all ten categories, not buying premium versions of each. A day hike that unexpectedly runs past dark or into bad weather is exactly the scenario this list is packed for.

title: Chemical Water Disinfection (Bleach, Iodine, Tablets)
summary: When boiling isn't possible, unscented household bleach, iodine, or chlorine dioxide tablets can disinfect small quantities of water - with real limits.
quick_actions: Plain, unscented household chlorine bleach (5-9% sodium hypochlorite, no added scents/dyes/cleaners) works: about 8 drops (roughly 1/8 teaspoon) per gallon of clear water, stirred and left to stand 30 minutes before use.

If the water is cloudy, filter it first through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter, or let it settle and draw off the clear water - cloudy water needs more disinfectant and is harder to treat reliably.
Chlorine dioxide tablets and iodine are alternatives, each with their own dosing on the product label - follow the product's own instructions rather than guessing a dose.
Chemical disinfection is weaker than boiling against the parasites Cryptosporidium and Giardia - boiling remains the more reliable method whenever it's possible.

None of this makes water safe if it is contaminated with fuel, other toxic chemicals, or radioactive material - use a different water source instead, and contact the local health department for guidance.
more_info: A portable filter rated for very small pore sizes (look for "absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller" on the label) can also remove many pathogens, though not viruses - combining filtration with a chemical disinfectant step covers more ground than either alone.
